1:
Gill begins with what the heading does not mean. These are not the ten commandments repeated from the preceding chapter but all the others, moral, ceremonial and judicial, afterwards declared; Moses gives a fresh declaration of laws already received, which is how the Targum of Jonathan paraphrases the clause — this is a declaration of the commandments, statutes and judgments. Ellicott presses the Hebrew, which has the first noun singular: this is the commandment, the statutes, and the judgments. The commandment is the duty imposed on Israel by the covenant of the ten words, its application to daily life, comprising statutes, meaning religious ordinances or institutions, and judgments, meaning actual rules of behaviour. Sometimes the two are only aspects of one thing. The Passover is a statute, what we should call an institution; the rules for keeping it are judgments. The thing itself is permanent, the rules may vary — it was eaten at first standing and in haste, and once Israel was at rest, reclining and in repose. Henry divides the three more simply: the commandments are the moral law, the statutes the ceremonial, the judgments the law by which the judges decided.

Ellicott also sets the verse in the shape of the book. The Decalogue recapitulated, Moses applies its principles to Israel's conduct in the land; this first part is the more general, concerning their relation to the God who brought them from Egypt, and runs to the end of the eleventh chapter. What follows is particular, concerning the land as the seat of the worship and kingdom of Jehovah — though the whole discourse is presented as one unbroken piece. Keil takes up the purpose stated next: the law was communicated to awaken the fear of God, and such a fear as would show itself at all times in keeping every commandment. He notices that thou and thy son is the subject of that clause but stands last for emphasis, and corrects a point of grammar — the verb rendered prolonged is not transitive, to make long, but intransitive, to last long. Clarke reduces the third verse to a sequence: God is to be heard, there being no obligation without a law to found it on and no law in religion but from God; the commandment must be understood to be obeyed, and observed to be understood; and it must be performed, that its end may be reached.

On the pastoral force Henry and Calvin converge from different directions. Henry notes that Moses taught all that, and only that, which God commanded — as Christ's ministers are to teach his churches all he has commanded, neither more nor less; that the whole end of teaching was doing, so that good instruction will only aggravate our condemnation if we do not live up to it; and that the entail of religion in a family or country is the best entail, it being desirable that not we only but our children's children should fear the Lord. Clarke makes the last point too: whoever fears God will endeavour to bring up his children in the same way, so that religion is kept in the family not in word only but in practice. Calvin reads the verses as an appeal to gratitude. God deals so liberally with Israel that they would be perverse if such kindness did not allure them to love the law; Moses sets the promised land before their eyes to prepare their minds for submission and make the rule of so bountiful a Father delightful. And he draws a sting from the repetition itself: it shows how hard it is for men to be prepared to keep the law, since God does not stimulate their indolence in vain, and there is a silent reproof of their sloth in the fact that he keeps insisting on what it should have been enough to say once.
4:
Gill explains the call for a hearing: Moses is stirring the people to attend to a momentous article, the unity of God, to keep them from polytheism and idolatry. From the opening word the Jews name the section Kiriath-shema, and recite it twice daily. Gill notes a scribal peculiarity — the last letters of the first and last words, Shema and Echad, are written larger than ordinary, which seems designed to excite attention. Keil reports the rabbinic explanation of those enlarged letters, the finest thing here. Taken together they spell a word meaning a witness. R. Bochin's inference is that a man may confess one God with his mouth while his heart is far from him; the letters are magnified so that whoever professes the divine unity should know his heart ought to be engaged and free of every other thought, God being himself a witness. Henry adds the liturgical warmth: the Jews reckon these verses among the choicest portions of scripture and count themselves not merely obliged but happy to say them daily, having the saying among them, Blessed are we, who every morning and evening say, Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God is one Lord.

On the translation Clarke is candid about the limits of certainty. The Hebrew may be rendered several ways — Jehovah, our God, is one Jehovah; or Jehovah is our God, Jehovah alone — and almost all the varieties, he says, come to the same sense. He notes this is one of the four passages written on the phylacteries, cites Maimonides that the words contain the property, the love and the doctrine of God, and thinks it perhaps in reference to that custom that our Lord called it the first commandment. On whether the verse teaches the Trinity in unity Clarke will not overclaim: many think it does, and it may be so, but no more clearly here than in the first verse of Genesis. He describes with some heat the synagogue practice of repeating the last word for minutes together, which he supposes aimed at Christians as holders of three gods, and answers that the plural form of the word rendered our God cannot be argued away. Henry makes the suggestion more mildly: some have thought there is a plain intimation of the trinity of persons in the unity of the Godhead, since the name of God stands here three times and is yet declared one.

Calvin insists the oneness is no abstraction. When Moses proclaims that God is one, the statement is not confined to his sole essence, which is incomprehensible, but is to be understood of the power and glory manifested to this people — as if to say they would be rebels unless they abode in the God who had laid them under such obligations. Hence Moses does not merely name him Jehovah but adds thy God, and by that all other deities are brought to nought. Then comes Calvin's sharpest stroke. A god may keep his name and yet be stripped of his majesty as soon as he is mixed with a multitude; so God says by Ezekiel, go ye, serve every one his idols — words in which he not only repudiates all mixed worship but testifies that he would rather be accounted nothing than not be worshipped undividedly. He adds that the orthodox Fathers used the verse against the Arians, since Christ is everywhere called God and must therefore be the same Jehovah who declares himself the one God, and the same holds of the Spirit. Keil marks the structural weight of the verse: here the burden of the law commences, not a new law added to the ten commandments but the unfolding of what lay in them as a germ, beginning with the first, and containing two things — that Jehovah is the one absolute God, and that he requires love with all the heart.
5:
Keil takes the three terms in order and finds a progression. The heart is named first as the seat of the emotions and of love; then the soul, as the centre of personality, which makes the love pervade the whole self-consciousness; then the strength, of body and soul together. With all the heart excludes half-heartedness, all division of the heart in loving; and the motive lies in the words thy God, Jehovah being Israel's God and having shown himself one. Loving him so stands at the head, Keil adds, as the principle from which keeping the commandments was to flow. Ellicott turns to a Jewish commentator, whose glosses are memorable. With all thy heart is expounded as with both natures, the good and the evil; with all thy soul as even though he take thy life from thee; and with all thy might, practically enough, as with all thy money — for you sometimes find a man whose money is dearer to him than his body. Ellicott grants the verbal connection will not hold, but thinks it a useful illustration. Wesley puts a question rather than an exposition: is this an external commandment only? Can any then say the Sinai covenant was merely external?

That the words must be in the heart Clarke treats as self-evident — where else can love be? If it is not in the heart it does not exist; and if these commands are not esteemed and prized as a glorious privilege, there is no hope love will reign there. Keil makes the same distinction more precisely: they were to be an affair of the heart and not merely of the memory. Calvin reads heart as covering memory and the other faculties, and hears an estimate of worth — so great a treasure that there was good cause to hide it in their hearts, fixing the doctrine so deeply it should never escape. On the word rendered teach diligently they converge, then divide. Gill, Clarke and Wesley all note that it means to whet or sharpen, a thing done by repeated friction, and take it for constant reiteration until the children are sharp in what they are taught. Calvin proposes something else. From the conjugation used he thinks the sense may be transitive — not that the doctrine is whetted by repetition, but that parents should cause it to penetrate their children's minds, as if pricking them with a sword's point. He offers it with unusual diffidence, as his own opinion only, lest anyone be offended by its novelty.

Calvin has the sharpest account of what went wrong with the frontlets. He takes them for a spiritual ornament set against chains of gold, as if a man should delight more in the pious recollection of the law than in trifles that catch the senses. The Jews, understanding it literally, made the external show a mark of holiness, as if all were nearly done when they wore the law on arms and forehead; and the zeal went further, each widening his phylacteries as he wished to be thought better than his neighbours — an error our Lord reproved severely, as mocking the admonition and profaning its doctrine. Keil arrives by another road: the commands being figurative and denoting undeviating observance, a literal fulfilment is praiseworthy only as a means of actually keeping what is written. Henry lists the means by which religion is kept up in hearts and houses — meditation, the education of children, pious discourse, frequent reading — and warns of what follows plenty: coming easily by the gift, men grow secure and unmindful of the Giver, so one must take care, lying safe and soft, not to forget the Lord. Ellicott adds that a parent should never hesitate to answer anything a child asks, and reflects that had such an education been carried on from the first, Israel's history would have been very different.
8:
Clarke hears in the binding a custom kept almost everywhere. When a man wishes to remember something important and dares not trust his memory, he ties a knot in his clothes or a cord on his finger, or sets something out of its place and in view, so that his memory may be whetted and his eye affect his heart. God, knowing how slow of heart we are, graciously orders us to use every help, and through things sensible to rise to things spiritual. Wesley says the same more shortly: use all means to keep them in remembrance, as men bind something on their hands or set it before their eyes to prevent forgetting what they wish to recall. The Jews took the words literally, and Gill describes both practices. For the hand, a scroll carrying this section and others, bound by the Targum of Jonathan upon the left hand — whence, Ellicott notes, the Tephillin, the portions of law bound on head or arm before prayer. For the doorposts, the parchment is written and rolled, the name Shaddai written outside, the roll put into a cane or hollow wood and fastened at the right hand of entrance; and as often as they go in and out they make it part of their devotion to touch and kiss it.

Clarke's rebuke of the custom falls on both sides. The Jews, forgetting the spirit and design of the precept, used these things as superstitious people use amulets, supposing that with such passages on slips of pure parchment, wrapped round the forehead, tied to the arm or nailed to the doorpost, they would be delivered from every evil. But how much better, he asks, are the many Christians who keep a Bible in the house merely to keep the devil out, or under their pillows to ward off spirits at night? How ingenious is the heart of man, Clarke concludes, to find out every wrong way and miss the right.

The warning against prosperity Calvin treats as foresight rather than suspicion. Wealth mostly blinds men's minds, so that instead of attending to modesty they grow wanton and intoxicate themselves with pleasure; God provides against this by anticipation, knowing it a common vice for abundance to beget arrogance — as the song afterwards puts it, Jeshurun waxed fat and kicked, and forsook God who made him. Calvin measures the ingratitude by the gift. It was inestimable goodness to give them cities built by other hands and transfer to them what others had prepared by great labour, so their impiety would be the more detestable in neglecting the Giver who set himself daily before them in that store of blessing. From which he draws the finest sentence in the passage: what ought to serve as vehicles to lift our minds on high are, by our own fault, turned into obstacles and clogs. He adds that Moses sets their new dominion against the house of bondmen, nothing being more likely to incline men to humility than the memory of the state they were rescued from. Keil describes not forgetting positively — fearing God, serving him, swearing by his name. Fear stands first as the fundamental note of Israelite worship, not slavish but the holy awe of a sinner before a holy God, which includes love rather than excludes it; fearing is of the heart, serving of working, and swearing in his name the practical showing of that worship in conversation, meaning not chiefly the oath before a court but the asseverations of ordinary life, in which a man's religion involuntarily reveals itself. Clarke ends on providence: in earthly prosperity men forget heavenly things, which is why God in love makes comparative poverty and frequent affliction the general lot — though extreme poverty, he grants, injures religion as much as excessive affluence, which is the wisdom of Agur's prayer for neither.
13:
Ellicott renders the clause with the Hebrew's own emphasis — Jehovah thy God thou shalt fear, and him shalt thou serve — that is, him only, as the Septuagint has it and as our Lord cited it in the temptation. And he makes an observation worth the whole note: every one of Christ's answers to the tempter was drawn not merely from Deuteronomy but from one and the same portion of it, the section from the fifth chapter to the tenth, precisely where the Decalogue's principles are applied to Israel's life. Clarke works the same ground textually and more anxiously. Our Lord quotes the verse as him only shalt thou serve, and Clarke infers the word for only stood anciently in the Hebrew, being in the Septuagint the quotation comes from, and in the Coptic, Vulgate and Anglo-Saxon. He cites Kennicott that without it the verse would not have been conclusive for the purpose our Lord advanced it, some men having worshipped false gods alongside the true. Then he states the difficulty against himself: the word is in no Hebrew text nor any manuscript yet discovered. Gill defines the fear required — not the slavish fear of hell but a filial reverence owed to the God who brought them from bondage into liberty and from misery into plenty, so that they should fear the Lord and his goodness.

On swearing Clarke notes the verb means properly to be full or satisfied, an oath appealing to God as witness. Ellicott sets it in patriarchal context — Laban appealed to the God of Nahor, Jacob swore by the fear of his father Isaac — and Wesley adds the condition: when there is a call and just cause, not by idols. Calvin analyses the two commands as one movement. Fear contains subjection, God's majesty keeping men in their place, and worship follows as the proof of piety. But the fear enjoined is voluntary, so that men moved by it want nothing but to obey; when he says God brings us under the yoke by a sense of his power he does not mean servile obedience is extorted, only that men cannot obey until fear has subdued them, their corruption always carrying contempt for religion.

Calvin explains why the command was needed: superstition stood on every side, and it was a destructive temptation that nobody anywhere subscribed to the law's doctrine, while every nation had some religion or its name. The one God's authority had to be so established that the Jews might dare despise what all the Gentiles believed. God is called jealous, he adds, because he permits no rivalry detracting from his glory; his dwelling among them is named partly to inspire terror and partly to reprove their ingratitude, should they forsake him and seek gods afar off. Clarke turns the word into a marriage: Jehovah has betrothed you as a bride to her husband, so be not unfaithful, lest the love that distinguished you turn to jealousy. Ellicott notes what is threatened is absolute extermination, by the fire of that jealousy. On Massah he and Clarke ask and answer alike — the people tempted God by the unbelieving question, is the Lord among us or not, after proofs enough of his kindness. Calvin traces it to its root: unbelief was the fountain, for neither relying on God's providence nor resting in his fatherly love they burst into impatience, and came to think God was not with them unless he complied with their lusts — whence it appears true piety cannot be severed from faith. Ellicott ends where the citations began. Even beside Satan on the giddy pinnacle our Saviour refused to doubt the care of Jehovah, and would not throw himself into the angels' arms to escape him, but endured as seeing him who is invisible. To that standard Israel was called, and did not always reach it.
17:
Henry and Wesley say the same thing in the same words, worth the repetition: negligence will ruin us, but we cannot be saved without diligence. Henry adds that it takes great care and pains to keep religion in its power, and offers two inducements: that such obedience is acceptable to God — right and good in his sight, and that is right and good indeed which is so in God's sight — and that it profits the obedient, securing the land, prosperity in it, and victory over those in the way. Ellicott sharpens what was at stake. There was no longer any question whether Israel would cross the Jordan; the question was how far the conquest would be carried and in what time, and that depended on their faithfulness — Judges makes plain their disobedience delayed it.

The child's question turns the chapter. Clarke, borrowing from Ainsworth, calls what follows a brief catechism containing the grounds of religion, and adds that Hebrew has no verb for to mean, so it says simply what is, as the seven thin ears are seven years of famine. Ellicott observes the three terms appear together first in the introduction to this discourse, and distributes them — the Decalogue is primarily the Torah, the charge following comes under testimony, statutes and judgments better describing the chapters from the eleventh to the twenty-sixth. Henry draws the best pastoral lessons here. All divine institutions have a certain meaning, and something great is designed in them; it concerns us to know it, that we may perform a reasonable service and not offer the blind for sacrifice; and it is good for children to enquire early into the intent of what they are trained up in, since an inquisitive child in divine things shows he is concerned and takes the means of coming to know. Parents must instruct those under their charge even when they do not ask, and much more be ready to answer when the question is put, since whoever asks may be hoped willing to receive.

The answer prescribed is a history, not an argument. Keil notes the instruction hinted at earlier is here explained: in reply to their sons the Israelites were to tell what the Lord had done in redeeming them from bondage and bringing them into the land, so awakening love in the younger generation. Calvin presses why redemption is the ground on which the law is commended. Its authority claims the more because it was not imposed before God had laid them under obligation, and it would have been too base to refuse God as Lawgiver knowing they had been purchased by him. He finds a twofold tie: God devoted them to himself not once only but confirmed his dominion by their continued possession of the land. Ellicott traces the reasoning to the message from Sinai — having seen what was done to the Egyptians and been borne on eagles' wings, they should be a peculiar treasure if they kept the covenant, the keeping of that law in that land being the final cause of their national existence. On the closing words Calvin is careful in two directions. The phrase for our good shows God had regard not only to his own rights but to their advantage, so rejecting the law would make them doubly ungrateful; and while keeping it is in itself righteousness, no man is justified by it — which arises from no defect in its doctrine but must be imputed to our guilt, we being aliens from the righteousness it contains. Keil renders the last verse to the same effect: their righteousness would consist in observing the law. Henry turns it evangelically: could we perfectly fulfil that one command of loving God with all the heart, and say we had never done otherwise, the law would justify us; since we cannot, sincere obedience is accepted through a Mediator.
25:
The closing promise divides them. Gill reads it strictly and turns it against itself: to have a justifying righteousness this way a man must keep all the commandments perfectly, not one excepted, without the least breach in thought, word or deed; and before the Lord, not as it appears to himself but as it appears to God, who sees the heart; and in the manner commanded, with all his heart and soul and strength. This is not possible for a sinful man, so righteousness cannot be by the law. Only Christ kept them so, and his obedience is our righteousness. Wesley takes the sentence another way. The Hebrew word for righteousness is very often put for mercy, and that sense agrees better both with scriptural usage — where mercy, and hardly ever righteousness, is said to be to us or with us — and with the argument just made, that God commanded these things for our good. Read so, the verse promises not a verdict but a continuance: as he has done us good, he will do more, and his mercy shall be with us for ever. Ellicott supplies philology supporting it. One Targum has it shall be merit to us, another merit laid up against the world to come, the Septuagint it shall be alms to us — a conjunction which explains why alms and righteousness stand as alternative readings in Matthew, and why the Jews call alms by the word for righteousness to this day.

Clarke steers between them. The righteousness meant is evidence that we are under the fear and love of God; Moses does not say it could be wrought without God's mercy, nor that they should purchase heaven by it, but that God required conformity to his will in all things, holy in heart and righteous in conduct. He then leaves the verse for an argument he cares about more. A maxim had lately been advanced, which he hopes is disowned by the body its authors belong to: that children should not be taught religion lest their minds be biased toward a creed, but left to themselves until capable of choosing. Clarke calls this flatly opposed to God's command, and diagnoses it: those who teach it show how little they are affected by the religion they profess, for if they felt it good for anything they would wish their children to have it. But he does not let the orthodox off. What of parents who hold a better faith and equally neglect to instruct their children? They are highly criminal, and if their children perish through that neglect, which is very probable, theirs is a dreadful account to give.

The exhortation that follows is the warmest writing in the chapter. Parents are to teach their children that there is one Lord, whom they must love with all their heart and soul and might. Because children are heedless and easily carried away by what they can see, Clarke tells parents to repeat and re-repeat, adding line upon line and precept upon precept, studying time and place so the labour is not thrown away. Show religion in its amiableness, he says; excite attention by exciting interest; show how good, how useful, how blessed it is — and whet these things on their hearts till the keenest edge is raised on the strongest desire, till the child can say, whom have I in heaven but thee, and none on earth I desire beside thee. Clarke closes by returning to the oath. The appeal to God, calling him to witness and record, is the whole spirit and essence of it, whatever the outward form — hand under the thigh, a book kissed, a hand held up. On that ground the raised hand in court is as formal an oath as any, and he asks why so many object to one form when the same thing is done in substance.
